content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB), medically referred to as menorrhagia, is characterized by excessively heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding that interferes with a woman's physical, emotional, social, or material quality of life. Normally, menstrual bleeding lasts 3 to 7 days with a blood loss of about 30-40 milliliters; HMB is often defined as losing more than 80 milliliters per cycle or bleeding that lasts longer than seven days. The physiological mechanism involves the complex interplay of hormonal regulation, endometrial (uterine lining) function, blood coagulation, and vascular factors. Common causes include hormonal imbalances, uterine fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, bleeding disorders, infections, and rarely, malignancies. Important synonyms include menorrhagia, excessive menstrual bleeding, and abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB)—though AUB also includes bleeding irregularities beyond volume or duration. Evaluating HMB requires detailed history, physical examination, and targeted investigations such as blood tests, ultrasound imaging, and sometimes endometrial biopsy to identify underlying causes. Management options range from medical therapies like hormonal treatments (combined oral contraceptives, progestins), tranexamic acid, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, to surgical approaches like endometrial ablation or hysterectomy in selected cases. Lifestyle factors including iron-rich nutrition and stress management play supportive roles in symptom control. Recognizing symptoms is crucial to address anemia risk and improve quality of life. While most causes are benign, medical evaluation is essential to exclude serious conditions and to tailor therapy safely. This module synthesizes current evidence and clinical guidelines, bridging foundational physiology with practical patient care considerations for heavy menstrual bleeding.

chunk_title: Definition and Clinical Description of Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB), also known as menorrhagia, refers to excessive or prolonged menstrual bleeding that interferes with a woman’s physical, emotional, social, or material quality of life. It typically involves menstrual blood loss of more than 80 milliliters per cycle or bleeding lasting longer than 7 days. Common terms used synonymously include excessive menstrual bleeding and abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), although AUB is a broader category that includes other menstrual irregularities.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Normal menstrual bleeding results from the cyclical shedding of the endometrium (uterine lining) regulated by the hormonal interplay of estrogen and progesterone. The process includes vasoconstriction of endometrial blood vessels, activation of coagulation pathways, and controlled tissue breakdown. A typical menstrual period lasts 3 to 7 days with an average blood loss of 30-40 milliliters.

chunk_title: Mechanisms and Causes of Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
content: Heavy menstrual bleeding arises when there is disruption in the normal balance of endometrial repair, hormonal regulation, or coagulation. Major causes include structural abnormalities such as uterine fibroids (leiomyomas), polyps, adenomyosis; hormonal disorders including anovulation; bleeding disorders like von Willebrand disease; intrauterine devices; infections; and rarely, malignancies such as endometrial carcinoma. Idiopathic cases, where no clear cause is found, are also common.

chunk_title: Risk Factors for Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
content: Risk factors for HMB include age (more common during adolescence and perimenopause), obesity, family history of bleeding disorders, use of hormonal contraception or anticoagulant medications, uterine abnormalities, and certain systemic diseases like liver or kidney disease. Awareness of these factors aids in risk stratification and targeted evaluation.

chunk_title: Symptoms and Impact on Quality of Life
content: Symptoms of heavy menstrual bleeding include visibly heavy or prolonged bleeding, passage of large blood clots, frequent changing of sanitary products, and symptoms of anemia such as fatigue, weakness, or shortness of breath. HMB can lead to absenteeism from work or school, reduced social interactions, and psychological distress.

content: Evaluation involves detailed menstrual history including duration, flow, and impact; physical examination focusing on pelvic and abdominal findings; laboratory tests such as complete blood count and coagulation studies; and imaging studies like pelvic ultrasound to identify structural causes. Endometrial sampling may be indicated in women over 35 or with risk factors for malignancy to exclude cancer.

chunk_title: Medical Management of Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
content: Medical treatments include hormonal therapies such as combined oral contraceptives and progestins to regulate cycles and reduce bleeding; tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic that reduces bleeding volume; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) which decrease prostaglandin-mediated bleeding; and treatment of underlying disorders such as bleeding abnormalities. Medical therapy is usually first-line, especially for women desiring fertility preservation.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: When medical management is ineffective or contraindicated, surgical treatments include endometrial ablation—destruction of the uterine lining to reduce bleeding—and hysterectomy, the removal of the uterus, which provides definitive treatment. Other surgeries target structural causes, such as myomectomy for fibroids. Surgical options depend on patient preference, reproductive plans, and overall health.

content: Lifestyle interventions involve adequate nutrition rich in iron to prevent or treat anemia, stress management, and maintaining a healthy weight. Supportive care includes counseling and education about menstrual hygiene management and monitoring symptoms to identify worsening conditions needing medical attention.

chunk_title: Safety Considerations and When to Seek Medical Care
content: Patients with heavy menstrual bleeding should seek medical care if they experience symptoms of anemia (extreme fatigue, dizziness), pass large clots frequently, or if bleeding worsens abruptly. Safety considerations include ruling out pregnancy-related bleeding, infections, or malignancy, and careful evaluation before starting hormonal or surgical treatments.

chunk_title: Common Misconceptions about Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
content: A common misconception is that heavy menstrual bleeding is normal and cannot be treated. Another is that only older women experience HMB. Some believe natural remedies alone can cure HMB, which is not supported by strong evidence. Educating patients about the clinical significance and management options improves outcomes.

chunk_title: Emerging and Uncertain Evidence in Heavy Menstrual Bleeding
content: Emerging evidence explores new hormonal agents, minimally invasive surgical techniques, and better diagnostic biomarkers to personalize treatment. However, the heterogeneity of causes challenges uniform treatment. Research continues on optimal management strategies balancing efficacy, safety, and fertility preservation.
